text: The GDP deflator issue is something mainstream media refuses to discuss. When nominal GDP grows but deflator is low, real GDP looks impressive. But if actual price levels are higher than what deflator captures, real growth is overstated. This is a legitimate methodological debate, not conspiracy theory. RBI and MoSPI should publish more granular reconciliation data.

As someone who works in energy policy, the DISCOM resistance to rooftop solar is structurally predictable. State utilities lose revenue when prosumers generate their own power. The subsidy disbursement bottleneck isn't accidental — it's DISCOMs protecting their billing base. Until state governments decouple DISCOM incentives from unit sales, uptake will remain artificially suppressed regardless of central scheme design.

Thread on the collegium impasse (1/6): The Constitution under Article 124 says judges of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President after consultation with such judges as the President may deem necessary. The word 'consultation' was reinterpreted by the SC itself in the Second and Third Judges Cases (1993, 1998) to mean 'concurrence'. So the collegium system is judge-made law, not textual constitutional mandate. (2/6) The executive returning files is arguably within its rights to seek reconsideration — once. But returning the same file after the collegium reiterates its recommendation? That's a constitutional convention being weaponised. (3/6) We now have 400+ vacancies across High Courts. Allahabad HC alone has pendency of 10 lakh+ cases. Litigants in mofussil districts are dying before their property disputes are resolved. (4/6) The real victim here is not the judge whose elevation is stalled. It's the farmer in Bulandshahr whose land acquisition case has been listed and delisted 23 times. (5/6) Both sides — judiciary and executive — are playing power games while the constitutional machinery rusts. NJAC was struck down. Fine. But what's the alternative accountability mechanism? (6/6) We need a transparent, time-bound appointment protocol. Not this shadow boxing between Raisina Hill and Tilak Marg.

I work in the energy sector (distribution side) and want to give some context on the net-metering debate. The frustration of rooftop solar owners is completely valid, but the DISCOM's position is also not entirely wrong. When 15-20% of feeders have high solar penetration, the reverse power flow creates real technical issues — transformer overloading, voltage fluctuation, protection relay miscoordination. The solution isn't to kill net-metering but to invest in smart grid infrastructure. The problem is that CAPEX for smart meters and grid upgrades isn't being factored into the tariff order. SERC needs to create a separate grid modernization surcharge rather than penalizing prosumers.

As a solar installer working primarily in Rajasthan's tier-2 towns — Sikar, Churu, Jhunjhunu — I can tell you the proposed net-metering export cap will directly impact our business and our customers. We've been selling 3-10kW systems to small shopkeepers and farmers on the promise of ₹3.80/unit export credit. If RERC reduces this to ₹2.50, the financial model breaks for systems above 5kW. Customers will downsize their installations, we lose revenue, and the state misses its solar rooftop targets. The patwari and tehsildar offices are already slow with land use certificates for rooftop projects — now add financial disincentive on top. Bahut mushkil ho jayega.

As a civil engineer with 18 years of experience in municipal water systems, let me explain what has likely happened in technical terms. The distribution network in most Tier-2 Indian cities uses CI (Cast Iron) pipes laid in the 1970s-80s. These have a design life of 30-40 years. When internal corrosion creates micro-fractures and the pipe is laid in proximity to a leaking sewer line — which is extremely common in unplanned urban extensions — negative pressure events (like pump shutdowns at night) cause sewer water to be sucked INTO the drinking water line. This is called cross-contamination via back-siphonage. It is entirely preventable with proper pressure monitoring and pipe replacement. This is 100% a governance and maintenance failure. The JE who signed off on annual inspections should be held criminally liable.

THREAD: What actually happened at the Bhandup pumping station last night and why the valve operator's negligence caused a cascade failure across 3 zones. 1/ The main 1200mm DI pipe burst near Jogeshwari-Vikhroli Link Road at approximately 2:47 AM. Standard protocol requires the duty valve operator to isolate the section within 15 minutes using the master shutoff at Kanjurmarg junction. 2/ The operator on duty — reportedly absent from his post — was unreachable for 47 minutes. By the time manual isolation happened, 18 MLD of treated water had flooded the JVLR underpass and surrounding basements. 3/ The booster pump at Vikhroli sub-station then ran dry for 22 minutes, causing cavitation damage to two of the three pump impellers. This is why restoration is taking 96 hours instead of the usual 12. The infrastructure failure is real but the human failure is worse.

Spoke to a retired MCGM hydraulic engineer today (he doesn't want to be named). He said the booster pump failures across 12 zones are NOT coincidental. When the main transmission pressure drops suddenly due to a burst, the booster pumps in residential buildings are designed to handle a certain pressure differential. But half the pumps in this city are running on expired AMC contracts with no maintenance. So when the main line pressure crashed, the pumps tried to compensate, overloaded, and tripped. THREAD: Why the CAG draft leak matters beyond this one minister (1/5) The conflict of interest disclosure framework in most Indian states is completely toothless. Form CI-7 or equivalent exists on paper but there is NO independent verification mechanism. The minister self-declares. That's it. (2/5) The CAG preliminary audit found the declaration register itself was 'not produced' during audit. Not missing - not produced. That's a deliberate act. (3/5) PAC summons are good but PAC has no enforcement power if the executive stonewalls. They can report to the House, that's all. (4/5) The real fix is mandatory third-party verification of conflict disclosures and automatic recusal triggers in the file management system. (5/5) Until then, every clearance involving a minister's family will depend entirely on that minister's personal ethics. Which, as we see, is not a reliable safeguard.

Thread on what actually went wrong (I work in water utility consulting, not for any govt): 1/ The burst point is at a 90° elbow joint — highest stress concentration in any pipeline. These need ultrasonic thickness testing every 3 years. Last test here: 2018. 2/ The booster pumps at Stations 4 and 7 failed because they're running on 2003-era SCADA with no redundancy. When the main burst, pressure sensors sent conflicting signals and pumps auto-tripped. Nobody overrode manually for 4 hours. 3/ Emergency valve closure protocol requires 2-person authorization. One officer was unreachable. The other didn't have the physical key. The key system hasn't been digitized despite a 2020 directive. This is what 'governance failure' actually looks like at the technical level.

The KERC draft regulation on EV charging tariffs (Case No. 71/2023) actually has a very sensible provision — RWAs can be classified as 'aggregated consumers' and get bulk LT tariff rates instead of individual domestic rates. The information asymmetry between regulators and citizens is the real problem here, not the tariff itself.
